abstract.p: Several researches have reported considerable levels of phnolic compounds (bisphenol A (BPA), benzophenones (BP-1, BP-3) and triclosan (TCS)) in cosmetic/beauty products. However, there is limited data regarding the exposure of female beauticians to harmful substances. The present research aimed to evaluate the exposure of female salon workers to these pollutants by quantifying their urinary levels. To achieve this, 50 female beauticians were selected as the exposed group (EG) and a control group (CG) consisting of 35 housewives. Urine specimens were collected and analyzed by chromatographic techniques to determine the pollutants content. It was found that all pollutants (BPA, BP-1, BP-3 and TCS) were frequently detected in the urine samples of female beauticians. It was also observed that the levels of these contaminants in the samples collected from this occupational group was significantly higher than housewives (Pvalue < 0. 05). The median of urinary BPA, BP-1, BP-3 and TCS concentrations for exposed subjects before the shift were 4.76, 2.57, 2.1 and 8.75 ng/mL, respectively. However, higher levels of these compounds were found in urine samples collected after the shift with medians of 5.25, 3.1, 2.65 and 11.96 ng/mL, respectively. For control group, these records were 1.66, 0.76, 0.22 and 2.12 ng/mL, respectively. Based on multiple linear regression (MLR) test, it was also showed that “cosmetic products usage” and “personal protective equipment (PPE)” are leadings factors contributing to the levels of BPA, BP-1, BP-3 and TCS detected in the urine of the female beauticians. These observations underscore the urgent necessity for more severe regulations and improved safety protocols to minimize exposure to hazardous chemicals in beauty salon settings.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The beauty industry is fast developing and the demand for cosmetics and beauty services especially by women is increasing1,2. Therefore, numerous career opportunities for women as beauticians in beauty salons are made around the world3. A wide variety of chemical cosmetic products are applied by beauticians to offer beauty services and therapies to their clients4. They are classified to corrective, maintenance and active cosmetics, cosmetics for personal cleansing, the skin, hair, integument care and embellishment5. These chemical cosmetic products, which play a prominent role in everyday beautification routines, are one of the sources of environmental chemical exposures across all women6,7. Multiple toxic ingredients and contaminants are utilized in the beauty products formulations including polydimethylsiloxane, octinoxate methoxycinnamate, butylated hydroxytoluene, butylated hydroxylanisole, nano titanium dioxide, nano zinc oxide, parabens, phthalates, BPA, formaldehyde, heavy metals, microplastics, TCS, and BP8,9. Many of these toxic ingredients have the ability of bioaccumulation and are persistent in the environment10.

Among these pollutants, BPA, triclosan (TCP), and benzophenones (BPs) were targeted for analysis in this work given their routine presence in cosmetic and personal care products, potential endocrine-disrupting properties, and relevance to human biomonitoring research11,12. BPA is frequently utilized in plastics and epoxy resins and has been reported in human urine in several population studies, reflecting its ubiquitous routes of exposure13. In addition to cosmetic products, other occupational factors such as routine glove use and handling of plastic-based equipment and containers in beauty salons may contribute to BPA exposure14. Triclosan is an antimicrobial phenolic compound frequently present in cosmetics and personal care items, and benzophenones (particularly BP-3) are used as ultraviolet (UV) filters in sunscreens and cosmetics, with documented occurrence in human urine biomarkers15.

Beauticians are occupationally exposed to high levels of these toxic chemicals via the daily use of the beauty products in their occupational environment16,17. Nasal route, cutaneous, and ingestion are pathways of consumer and beautician’s exposure to the toxic chemicals4. The presence of the toxic chemicals in hazardous beauty products is a risk to consumers and beauticians’ health18,19. Most toxic chemicals are possible xenoestrogen to human such as BPA, TCP and BP derivatives that may disrupt the endocrine system20,21. BP derivatives such as BP-1and BP-3 have been identified as “possibly carcinogenic to humans”22. In addition, respiratory disorders23, eye and skin irritation, allergic reaction24, genotoxic effects25, breast cancer26, and reproductive and developmental complications27,28 have been reported to be associate with occupational chemical exposures of beauticians.

Our previous research study showed that BTEX compounds were released in indoor environment via the used cosmetics in beauty salons29. Other previous studies showed that occupational chemical exposures of female beauticians because of the high consumption of beauty and hygiene products resulted in the detection of parabens30, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs)31, and trace elements32 in their urinary samples. There are many studies that have reported the urinary levels of toxic chemicals concerning the application of cosmetics and personal care products in various populations5,33–38. According to the information available, there has been no study to measure the urinary concentrations of BPA, TCP, and BPs among women working as cosmetologists. In this regards, the present study was designed for first time to achieve the following aims: (1) measuring BPA, TCP, and BPs urinary concentrations of the female cosmetologists (2) estimating the occupational exposure level of the female cosmetologists, and (3) assessing the potential impact of socio-demographic and job-related factors on the urinary concentrations of the investigated compounds.

sec.title: Study participants and sampling procedure
sec.p: This research coded beauty salons throughout Bushehr city from 1.00 to 83.00 and then randomly selected 50.00 cases using Eq. (1):

Following that, the Bushehr trade union organization provided the addresses and information of the chosen salons. Female cosmetologists (n = 50.00) with a minimum of one year of ongoing employment in beauty salons were considered as the exposed group (EG). This criterion was applied to ensure prolonged and regular occupational exposure to cosmetic products and salon-related chemical substances, thereby making a more reliable evaluation of long-term exposure to phenolic compounds. Moreover, 35.00 individuals who identified as housewives were recruited as control group (CG). To select control group members, researchers visited homes in different areas, explaining the study and attempting to persuade women to participate. Women in the control group neither current nor past work experience in beauty salons or similar cosmetic occupations and reported no use of cosmetic products for a minimum of three weeks prior to urine sampling. This washout period was applied to reduce possible background exposure and leftover contamination from personal care products, ensuring that urinary phenolic compound levels in the control group reflected normal environmental exposure instead of recent cosmetic use. Those with medical conditions or taking medication were not eligible. This was done to remove any potential impact on the findings. In summary, all participants were healthy. Then, we went through making clarifications and providing additional information to get the sampling permit from the managers, owners, and staff of the salons. Following the participants’ signature on formal consent agreement, they were educated on the correct manner of biological sample collection, which also involved a detailed explanation of the optimal technique for avoiding cross-contamination. Sampling procedures were initiated and each participant have been provided with two urine collection containers; one is to be filled before their working shift as a fasting specimen, while the other occurs once their shift has finished. The specimens were collected before exposure (BE) and after exposure (AE) were gathered at dawn and following the end of their workday, respectively, utilizing 100-ml polyethylene receptacles high‑density polyethylene (HDPE) receptacles free of BPA, TCP, and BPs to minimize contamination risk. All containers were pre‑treated and verified for cleanliness to minimize external contamination from external sources prior to sampling. Urine specimen collection for the control group was limited to mid-morning (between 9:00 and 11:00 a.m.) to reduce the effects of diurnal variation. Once labeled and coded, the obtained specimens were promptly transported to the lab in a refrigerated state using a cold box filled with dry ice to maintain a low temperature. The specimens were adequately packed and refrigerated at − 20 °C until the final analyzes. The sampler received specific training in the collection, handling, and transportation of urine samples to guarantee compliance with strict protocols that minimize contamination and preserve sample integrity for the accurate analysis of phenolic compounds. Alongside the sampling procedure, we recorded the relevant background facts of each salon, encompassing the daily volume of services, ventilation, besides the length from the salons and nearby traffic. In addition, a checklist that was pre-designed in advance by the study team was employed to collect occupational and lifestyle data of the donors included in the sample. Table S1 provides information regarding the salons and their participants. The Research Ethics Committee of Bushehr Province University of Medical Sciences (BPUMS) approved the research protocol (approval ID: IR.BPUMS.REC.1402.266), and all procedures were conducted in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations. As well as, informed consent was obtained from all participants.

sec.title: Sample preparation and analysis
sec.p: The samples were prepared for the analysis of the target pollutants (BPA, TCS, BP-1 and BP-3) according to the method provided by Moos et al.39. For this, urine samples placed at -20 °C were placed at room temperature to defreeze. After it came out of the frozen state, it was gently stirred until they were homogenous. Then, about 250 µL of urine samples were poured into a 2-mL colored glass vial with screw cap. Thereafter, 250 µL of 1 M ammonium acetate buffer; 20 µL of internal standard (previously prepared in acetonitrile) and 5 µL of ß-glucuronidase/arylsulfatase solution were added to hydrolyze conjugated species. The total concentration of each analyte, encompassing both free and conjugated species, was determined. Then, this mixture was incubated for 4 h at 37 °C and was frozen overnight to precipitate cryophobic proteins. Then, the samples were thawn and centrifuged at 3500 for 10 min. After this step, the sample was placed in a stationary state and then the supernatant was removed and poured into a 2-mL glass vial with a screw cap. Finally, in order to determine the amount of target analytes, 100 µL of the sample was injected to a high-performance liquid chromatography system coupled with mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS, Agilent, USA) equipped with a C18 column (15 × 4.6 mm, 5.0 μm particle size, Phenomenex, USA).

sec.title: Quality assurance and quality control (QA/QC)
sec.p: Because of the widespread presence of the target contaminants, we are forced to identify and minimize any potential external sources of contaminants. For this purpose, all reagent used in the lab was screened and those with small amounts of pollutants were substituted with free reagents. All equipment used were prewashed with appropriate solvents (acetone/acetonitrile) and also, all testers and equipment operators involved in different stages of sample analysis strictly avoided using personal care products that contained TCS or other target analytes. Despite all these precautions, small amounts of contaminants could be detected for certain target analytes due to different and scattered sources (indoor dust). To solve this challenge, we prepared and analyzed blank samples in parallel with the main samples, and the values ​​observed in the blank samples were appropriately subtracted from the main samples. The guidelines provided by Food and Drug Administration (FDA)40 for the analysis of biological samples were used for method validation in the present study. According to this method, urine samples were fortified with reference standards along with isotope-labeled standards. The limit of detection (LOD) and limit of quantification (LOQ) ​​were calculated by repeating measurements at low spike values, respectively, with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 3 and 9. For quality control, standard solutions (0.5–80 ng/mL) were prepared and the HPLC-MS was calibrated in this selected range. In cases where the urinary pollutant levels among beauty salon women were greater than this concentration range, dilution is done with distilled water and re-analyzed. The relative standard deviations (RSDs) of repeated analyzes of standard solutions at varying levels (1.0, 5.0 and 20.0 ng/mL) were calculated and served as a metric to evaluate the accuracy of the analytical method. Intra-day precision was evaluated through six repeated tests of the standard solution at different time points within a single day at specific time intervals, while inter-day precision was evaluated through analyses conducted across six successive days. The recovery percentage (accuracy) of the analytical method was also determined via analysis of spiked samples at three different concentration points (1.0, 5.0 and 20.0 ng/mL) for each of the target analytes.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was carried out using STATA14.0 software (Stata, College Station, TX, USA). Mean and standard deviation (SD) for continuous variables are reported. To evaluate standard distribution variables, Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests and histograms were employed. Because BPA, BP-1, BP-3, and TCS concentrations were not normal, they were natural log-transformed and included in multiple linear regression models. Also, the association was measured using the Mann-Whitney U test among categorical and continuous variables examined in this research. Multiple linear regression models were used to estimate factors associated with mean BPA, BP-1, BP-3, and TCS in urine samples. Variables with a p-value less than 0.25 in the univariate analysis were included in the final models.

sec.title: Demographics of exposed and control group
sec.p: The chosen attributes of the studied participants are summarized in Table S1. The number of female beauticians’ involved in the analysis was 50. Half of the women (50%) did not finish their education and a majority (70%) were aged less than 40 years. 82% of the exposed subject was found to be at normal weight, according to World Health Organization (WHO). Only 26% of beauticians didn’t use the PPE. These women were predominantly tobacco use (76%), about one third (28%) of them were exposed to environmental tobacco smoke (second- and third-hand tobacco smoke) at home and 14% of them consumed alcohol. 58% of these people wear makeup more than twice a week. 68, 78, 66, and 68% of these people used shampoo, soap, cream, and lotion more than twice a week, respectively. Also, 82 and 84% of people used toothpaste/mouthwash and perfume/deodorant/body spray more than twice a day, respectively. Other characteristics of the work environment (including ventilation, distance from the high-traffic area, and number of services per day) are also given in Table S1.

sec.title: Analytical method validation
sec.p: The data obtained for the values ​​of average recovery, precision (intra-day and inter-day), LOD and LOQ for each of the target compounds (BPA, TCS, BP-1 and BP-3) are presented in Table S2. The calculated LOD values ​​for BPA, TCS, BP-1 and BP-3 are 0.18, 0.34, 0.21 and 0.67 ng/mL, respectively, and the LOQ values ​​for these compounds were also calculated 0.54, 1.02, 0.64 and 2.23 ng/mL, respectively. Recovery values ​​were obtained in the range of 106.2–88.5%. The intra-day and inter-day precision values ​​were obtained in the range of 6.6–1.5 and 1.7–7.4 ng/ml, respectively. These findings are consistent with the values ​​reported in previous studies39,41,42.

sec.title: Urinary levels of target analytes (BPA, BP-1, BP-3 and TCS)
sec.p: Target pollutants concentrations in urine specimen from an exposed group (n = 50) both before and after a work shift and a control group (n = 35) are provided in Figs. 1, 2, 3 and 4; Table 1. As seen, the urinary level (mean ± sd) of BPA for exposed subjects before and after the shift were 8.66 ± 7.05 and 10.22 ± 8.86, respectively, respectively, compared to 1.91 ± 0.88 ng/mL in control subjects. These records for BP-1 analysis were 3.78 ± 2.80, 5.30 ± 4.20, 0.90 ± 0.60 ng/mL and also for BP-3 were 2.19 ± 1.36, 2.64 ± 1.56, 0.26 ± 0.11 ng/mL, respectively. Similarly, the concentration (mean ± sd) of TCS concentration in pre- and post- shift urine samples of exposed subjects and in control subjects’ urine samples were 8.82 ± 6.68, 14.69 ± 12.43, 2.53 ± 1.55 ng/mL, respectively. Clearly, the exposed group exhibited higher levels of all target biomarkers compared to control group (P < 0.05). Also, the pollutants level in exposed group demonstrated a notable escalation from pre-shift to post-shift measurements, indicating the significant exposure of this occupational group to pollutants related to cosmetic-sanitary products43,44. From a health perspective, the detected concentrations of BPA and TCS in urine among the exposed participants are comparable to or exceed levels reported in previous biomonitoring evidences known to cause endocrine-disrupting effects, reproductive toxicity, and metabolic disorders45. Although there are no established global biological exposure limits for these pollutants, numerous studies have suggest that higher urinary BPA levels and triclosan levels might contribute to endocrine and inflammatory disturbances46. In another words, this highlighted difference indicates that exposure to cosmetic products results in an elevation of endocrine disrupting substances (e.g., BPA, BP-1, BP-3 and TCS), which may interfere with hormonal regulation and increase long-term adverse health outcomes such as reproductive dysfunction, thyroid disorders, and immune system alterations47,48. These findings also suggests that regular exposure to chemicals in beauty products such as beauty and skincare products, natural wellness items, and over-the-counter medications49 though working in beauty salons can causes an accumulation of TCS. There have been several studies conducted on the urinary levels of BPA in women so far. For example, within a nationwide longitudinal biomonitoring research conducted in pregnant women from different sites across, the geometric mean of BPA and triclosan in urine were 0.80 and 21.64 ng/mL, respectively50. Moreover, in a research carried out with 80 pregnant women (≥ 18 years old) from the Ottawa area, the geometric mean of urinary BPA and triclosan concentrations were reported as 1.1 µg/L and 21.60 ng/mL, respectively51. Compared with these reference populations, the beauticians in this study showed significantly elevated BPA levels, suggesting an occupational source in addition to general environmental exposure. Ahra Ko et al.48 investigated the urinary concentrations of BP in 168 Korean adults (male = 89, female = 79) using personal care products (PCPs) and the their findings revealed that the mean levels of BP-1 and BP-3 were 0.87 and 5.87ng/g creatinine, respectively. This study also reported that the geometric mean levels of BP-1 and BP-3 were meaningfully greater in female than those in male48. In another study carried out in China, the urinary concentration of BP-1 and BP-3 were determined to be 0.38 and 0.39 µg/L, respectively52. Based on these findings, it can be inferred that the occupational exposure of beauticians to PCPs is strongly associated with some endocrine disruptors (e.g., BPA, BP-1, BP-3 and TCS) levels in human biological matrixes48.

sec.title: Affecting factors and urinary levels of target pollutants
sec.p: The unadjusted analysis concerning the relationship among the study variables and the concentration of BPA, BP-1, BP-3, and TCS in the urine samples of female beauticians is presented in Table 2. The results indicated that no meaningful difference exists in the biomarkers concentration among age groups (P > 0.05). The obese group was found to have higher mean level of BPA and BP-1 in the BMI groups (P < 0.05). No significant association was observed between the BPA, BP-1, BP-3, and TCS levels and education status (P > 0.05). An association between the period of employment and BPA, BP-1, BP-3, and TCS concentrations was observed (P < 0.001). We also observed in previous studies that work history (the number of years a person has been working in a beauty salon) can be a determining factor in the urinary levels of hazards such as PAHs, parabens, and potentially toxic elements53–55. These results show that the duration of exposure to the working environments of beauty salons can directly affect the level of these pollutants in the body. There was a significant association between the quantity of services per work shift and urinary level of BPA, BP-1, BP-3, and TCS biomarkers (P < 0.001). With the increase in the number of indoor services, higher amounts of personal care materials and cosmetics are used in these salons, and as a result, more pollutants are released into the air inside these salons and expose the beauticians56,57. As shown in Table 2a significantly higher mean of BPA, BP-1, BP-3, and TCS are observed in women who use makeup and cream (P < 0.001). The mean levels of BPA, BP-1, BP-3, and TCS in women who use lotion twice a week was considerably greater than in the group who use lotion less than twice a week(P < 0.001). Several studies have shown that cosmetic-health products (such as creams, lotions, etc.) may contain a wide range of potentially dangerous chemicals such as volatile organic compounds, parabens, BPA, aromatics, TCS, phthalate esters, ketones, aromatic terpenes, be camphor and ammonium57–59. These materials are released into the indoor air and remain in the environment when providing cosmetic services in beauty salons. Finally, people who use these products consistently or spend a lot of time in environments with high consumption of these substances (such as beauty salons) are exposed to higher amounts of these chemical pollutants, which can pose potential health risks to them60,61.

sec.p: The results of the adjusted linear regression model examining the relationship between the research variables and BPA, BP-1, BP-3, and TCS are presented in Table 3. The findings from multiple linear regression indicated that female beauticians who use PPE had a significant negative effect on BPA levels. (β yes/no = -0.55, 95%CI:-1.07 to -0.03, P = 0.039). In the field visits of this study, it was observed that some women working in beauty salons use equipment such as N95 masks, surgical masks, gloves, face shields, and similar items during the provision of beauty services. These equipment can lead to the reduction of people’s exposure to pollutants released from cosmetics and as a result, lower amounts of these pollutants can be observed in their biological samples62. In fact, the use of these protective equipment plays a crucial role in reducing the health hazards related to chemicals in cosmetic products. The mean BPA (β>2/<2 = 0.84, 95%CI: 0.31 to 1.37, P = 0.002) and BP-1 (B> 2/<2 = 0.81, 95%CI: 0.16 to 1.47, P = 0.016) were higher among women who use of mouthwash and toothpaste more than twice a week. Using creams more than twice a week had a positive association with BPA (β>2/<2 = 0.70, 95%CI: 0.17 to 1.23, P = 0.011), BP-1(β>2/<2 = 0.73, 95%CI: 0.10 to 1.36, P = 0.024), and BP-3(β>2/<2 = 0.78, 95%CI: 0.02 to 1.53, P = 0.042), levels in female beauticians’ urine samples. A scientific report by Iribarne-Durán et al.63, has shown that the use of mouthwash and hair coloring might be connected with an increase in the amount of BPA in the body of lactating women. The findings of their study indicated that hygiene and cosmetic products, such as mouthwash and hair dye, can act as non-food sources of BPA in the body of lactating women and, as a result, affect the amount of this chemical in breast milk63. In addition, women who use makeup more than twice a week experience a higher level of BPA (β>2/<2 = 0.53, 95%CI: 0.02 to 1.04, P = 0.039), BP-1(β>2/<2 = 0.71, 95%CI: 0.07 to 1.34, P = 0.028), and TCS (β>2/<2 = 0.78, 95%CI: 0.09 to 1.65, P = 0.029). Studies have shown that makeup products such as lipstick, nail polish, liquid foundation and other similar items can contain significant amounts of various pollutants such as parabens, BPA, BP-1, BP-3 and TCS64–66. Therefore, by increasing the number of times these products are used, a person enters his body through skin absorption and sometimes ingestion of these toxic substances, and as a result, higher amounts of them can be identified in biological matrices. A significant and positive correlation was detected between the urinary amount of BP-1(β>2/<2 = 1.46, 95%CI: 0.80 to 2.12, P < 0.001), BP-3(β>2/<2 = 0.93, 95%CI: 0.21 to 1.65, P = 0.012), and TCS (β>2/<2 = 1.35, 95%CI: 0.55 to 2.14, P = 0.001) and lotions usage in female beautician. In a study by Liao et al.59, body lotions were found to contain significant concentrations of triclosan, reaching approximately 3000 ng/g. The use of these lotions can expose a person to triclosan through skin absorption and thus lead to possible risks associated with this chemical.

sec.title: Limitations and ideas for future studies
sec.p: The current study, despite its innovative and valuable findings, has limitations that we decided to point out in this section so that researchers can consider them in the design of future studies. First, the low sample size in this investigation might limit the generalizability of the findings for beauty salons in different countries and cities worldwide, Therefore, additional researches must be carried out with more precision and involve a greater number of samples. Second, the exposure to the target compounds (BPA, BP-1, BP-3 and TCS) can vary across different locations and time periods. Third, in this study we did not differentiate between conjugated and non-conjugated species, which could have influenced the results. Forth, cosmetic and sanitary product use is not the only source of human exposure to these pollutants, as other sources such as drinking water, food packaging materials, and dietary habits might play a crucial role as well. Our checklist did not account for these factors, which should be considered in future research. Moreover, other work-related practices, such as the frequency and type of glove usage in beauty salons, could play a role in BPA exposure levels and were not specifically evaluated in the current research. Therefore, a more comprehensive and detailed research is needed regarding these pollutants, including analyses of food, water, and other relevant samples in these salons. These contaminants can result in health issues, including changes in inflammatory factors and increased oxidative stress, in exposed individuals. Therefore, it is suggested carrying out an in-depth analysis on the mechanisms of inflammatory/oxidative stress resulting from exposure to these pollutants in female beauticians.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This work provides the first published evidence of some cosmetic-related chemicals in urine from a female beauticians. BPA, BP-1, BP-3 and TCS were commonly quantified in urine specimens, and statistical analysis showed positive links between their urinary levels and certain occupational/ lifestyle parameters, particularly the regular use of specific cosmetic products (e.g., makeup ingredients, face creams, mouthwash and toothpaste, lotions). These findings, which need validation through more researches with greater number of samples, point to an urgent need to detect chemical levels in urine and to apply preventive monitor to reduce exposure for female beauticians. Moreover, there was a significant negative correlation among PPE utilization and urinary levels of BPA. Therefore, ensuring that beauticians in these salons are properly equipped and use PPE correctly may cause a substantial decrease in the level of contaminants in their biological samples and ultimately reduce the prevalence of occupational diseases.
